items.question: Why do the Danites look for a place to live?
items.answer: The Danites have not yet received a share among Israel.

window_text.1: In those days Israel had no king. And in those days the tribe of the Danites was seeking a place of their own where they might settle, because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
window_text.2: So the Danites sent five of their leading men from Zorah and Eshtaol to spy out the land and explore it. These men represented all the Danites. They told them, “Go, explore the land.” So they entered the hill country of Ephraim and came to the house of Micah, where they spent the night.

items.original_question: Why do the Danites look for a place to live?
items.original_answer: The Danites have not yet received a share among Israel.

assessments.reason: The passage explicitly says they were seeking a place to settle “because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel,” which matches the key’s “not yet received a share among Israel.”

blind.reason: The text directly gives the reason: they had not yet received an inheritance/share among Israel.

editor.quote: because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
editor.contrast: The stated cause—the Danites had not received an inheritance—versus the background fact that Israel had no king.
editor.reason: Israel’s lack of a king could be mistaken for the cause, but the explicit “because” clause uniquely identifies why the Danites were seeking a place to settle. The key accurately paraphrases that cause.

reader.quote: because they had not yet come into an inheritance among the tribes of Israel.
reader.contrast: Their lack of an inheritance among Israel’s tribes versus Israel’s having no king.
reader.reason: The explicit “because” clause identifies not yet having an inheritance as the reason they were seeking somewhere to settle. The statement that Israel had no king is background, not the stated cause.

items.question: Who tells the men near Micah’s house about Micah’s actions?
items.answer: The young Levite tells the men near Micah’s house.
items.competitor: Micah tells the men near Micah’s house.

window_text.3: When they were near Micah’s house, they recognized the voice of the young Levite; so they turned in there and asked him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?”
window_text.4: He told them what Micah had done for him, and said, “He has hired me and I am his priest.”

items.original_question: Who tells the men near Micah’s house about Micah’s actions?
items.original_answer: The young Levite tells the men near Micah’s house.

blind.question: Who tells the men near Micah’s house about Micah’s actions?

readings.support: the young Levite | He told them what Micah had done for him
He told them what Micah had done for him | I am his priest

assessments.reason: Verse 3 identifies “the young Levite,” and verse 4 says “He told them what Micah had done for him,” so the young Levite is the one who tells them.
The speaker adds, “I am his priest,” identifying himself as Micah’s priest; this is the same young Levite who told them what Micah had done.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly says the young Levite—who is also Micah’s priest—told them what Micah had done.

editor.quote:
the young Levite; so they turned in there and asked him, “Who brought you here? What are you doing in this place? Why are you here?”
4  He told them what Micah had done for him
editor.contrast: The young Levite as the person telling the men versus Micah as the person whose actions are being reported.
editor.reason: Micah could be mistaken for the speaker because his actions are the subject of the report. However, the men address the young Levite, and the following “He told them” continues with that same person. The wording clearly asks for the teller, so the key is uniquely supported.

reader.quote: He told them what Micah had done for him
reader.contrast: The young Levite is the speaker; Micah is the person whose actions he reports.
reader.reason: The men address the young Levite, and the following “He” refers to him. The question tests whether the reader distinguishes the person telling the story from the person being discussed.

items.question: Who is asked to consult God?

window_text.5: Then they said to him, “Please inquire of God to learn whether our journey will be successful.”
window_text.6: The priest answered them, “Go in peace. Your journey has the Lord’s approval.”

items.original_question: Who is asked to consult God?

blind.question: Who is asked to consult God?

readings.support: Please inquire of God | The priest answered them

assessments.reason: In v5 they speak to “him,” and v6 clarifies “The priest answered them,” identifying the one asked to consult God as the priest.

blind.reason: Verse 6 identifies the “him” of verse 5 as “the priest,” matching the key.

reader.quote: The priest answered them, “Go in peace. Your journey has the Lord’s approval.”
reader.contrast: The priest is the person asked to inquire; God is the one he is asked to consult.
reader.reason: The priest’s immediate answer identifies him as the antecedent of “him.” The question clearly tests the recipient of the request rather than merely retrieving a word.

editor.contrast: the priest, who was asked to inquire, versus God, whom he was asked to consult
editor.reason: The request is addressed to “him,” and the next line identifies the respondent as the priest. God is the object of the inquiry, not the person being asked.

items.question: Why are the people at Laish well-off?
items.competitor: Because they are at peace and secure.

window_text.7: So the five men left and came to Laish, where they saw that the people were living in safety, like the Sidonians, at peace and secure. And since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous. Also, they lived a long way from the Sidonians and had no relationship with anyone else.
window_text.8: When they returned to Zorah and Eshtaol, their fellow Danites asked them, “How did you find things?”

items.original_question: Why are the people at Laish well-off?

blind.question: Why are the people at Laish well-off?

readings.support: since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous.

assessments.reason: The text explicitly states, “since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous,” directly matching the answer that they are well-off because their land lacked nothing.

blind.reason: The passage explicitly links their prosperity to the land lacking nothing: “since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous.”

reader.quote: since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous.
reader.contrast: The cause of their prosperity—the land lacked nothing—versus their separate condition of being peaceful and secure.
reader.reason: The causal word “since” directly links the land’s abundance to their prosperity. Peace and security describe how they lived but are not stated as the reason they were well-off.

editor.quote: since their land lacked nothing, they were prosperous.
editor.contrast: Their prosperity comes from the land lacking nothing, not merely from their being peaceful and secure.
editor.reason: The causal wording “since” directly identifies why they were prosperous. The question clearly asks for that cause, requiring the reader to distinguish prosperity from the separate description of their safety.

items.question: From what place do the Danites continue toward the hill country?
items.answer: From the camp near Kiriath Jearim.

window_text.11: Then six hundred men of the Danites, armed for battle, set out from Zorah and Eshtaol.
window_text.12: On their way they set up camp near Kiriath Jearim in Judah. This is why the place west of Kiriath Jearim is called Mahaneh Dan to this day.
window_text.13: From there they went on to the hill country of Ephraim and came to Micah’s house.

items.original_question: From what place do the Danites continue toward the hill country?
items.original_answer: From the camp near Kiriath Jearim.

blind.question: From what place do the Danites continue toward the hill country?

readings.answer: Mahaneh Dan, west of Kiriath Jearim

set up camp near Kiriath Jearim in Judah | From there they went on to the hill country

assessments.reason: The text names the place west of Kiriath Jearim as Mahaneh Dan and then says “From there they went on to the hill country,” which is the same camp near Kiriath Jearim referenced by the key.
“Set up camp near Kiriath Jearim in Judah” followed by “From there they went on” directly matches the key’s “From the camp near Kiriath Jearim.”

blind.reason: “From there they went on” clearly refers back to the camp near Kiriath Jearim (called Mahaneh Dan), so both readings match the key.

reader.quote: From there they went on to the hill country of Ephraim
reader.contrast: The immediate departure point—the camp near Kiriath Jearim—versus the Danites’ earlier origin in Zorah and Eshtaol.
reader.reason: “From there” refers to the camp near Kiriath Jearim in the preceding verse, so the key correctly identifies where they continued from.

editor.quote:
On their way they set up camp near Kiriath Jearim in Judah. This is why the place west of Kiriath Jearim is called Mahaneh Dan to this day.
13  From there they went on to the hill country of Ephraim
editor.contrast: The immediate departure point for the hill country versus the Danites’ earlier starting point at Zorah and Eshtaol.
editor.reason: Zorah and Eshtaol are a plausible alternative because the journey began there, but “From there” refers to the most recently stated location, their camp near Kiriath Jearim. The question and key correctly resolve that reference.

items.question: Which men go inside and take the idol?
items.answer: the five men who had spied out the land
items.competitor: the six hundred Danites, armed for battle

window_text.14: Then the five men who had spied out the land of Laish said to their fellow Danites, “Do you know that one of these houses has an ephod, some household gods and an image overlaid with silver? Now you know what to do.”
window_text.15: So they turned in there and went to the house of the young Levite at Micah’s place and greeted him.
window_text.16: The six hundred Danites, armed for battle, stood at the entrance of the gate.
window_text.17: The five men who had spied out the land went inside and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods while the priest and the six hundred armed men stood at the entrance of the gate.

reader.reason: The window explicitly identifies the five spies as the actors who went inside and took the idol, distinguishing them from the six hundred men standing outside.

items.question: Who tells the priest to be quiet?

window_text.18: When the five men went into Micah’s house and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
window_text.19: They answered him, “Be quiet! Don’t say a word. Come with us, and be our father and priest. Isn’t it better that you serve a tribe and clan in Israel as priest rather than just one man’s household?”
window_text.20: The priest was very pleased. He took the ephod, the household gods and the idol and went along with the people.
window_text.21: Putting their little children, their livestock and their possessions in front of them, they turned away and left.

items.original_question: Who tells the priest to be quiet?

readings.support: the five men | They answered him, “Be quiet!

assessments.reason: Verse 19 says “They answered him, ‘Be quiet!’” and the antecedent of “They” in verse 18 is “the five men,” so the five men tell the priest to be quiet.

blind.reason: “They answered him, ‘Be quiet!’” clearly refers to the five men mentioned immediately prior.

editor.quote:
When the five men went into Micah’s house and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
19  They answered him, “Be quiet!
editor.contrast: The five men are the speakers, while the priest is the person being told to be quiet.
editor.reason: The dialogue turn resolves the roles: the priest asks the five men a question, and “They answered him” identifies those men as the speakers of “Be quiet!” This requires tracking speaker versus recipient rather than merely retrieving a nearby word.

reader.quote:
When the five men went into Micah’s house and took the idol, the ephod and the household gods, the priest said to them, “What are you doing?”
19  They answered him, “Be quiet!

reader.reason: “They” refers back to the five men, while “him” refers to the priest. The reader must distinguish the speakers from the recipient of their command.
